redox-reactions-s1.title: Metals in metal-ion solutions
redox-reactions-s1.text: A student places a clean strip of each metal into 1 M solutions of the nitrates of the other metals and watches for a coating or other change after 10 minutes. Nitrate ions take no part in any of the reactions.

table.caption: Observations (✓ = coating forms and metal strip slowly dissolves; – = no change)

redox-reactions-s2.title: A redox titration
redox-reactions-s2.text:
A student pipets 25.00 mL of an acidified Fe²⁺ solution into a flask and titrates it with 0.02000 M KMnO₄. The purple MnO₄⁻ ion is reduced to nearly colorless Mn²⁺, so the first lasting pale pink color marks the end point; no separate indicator is needed. The balanced net ionic equation is

MnO₄⁻(aq) + 5Fe²⁺(aq) + 8H⁺(aq) → Mn²⁺(aq) + 5Fe³⁺(aq) + 4H₂O(l)

items.q: Which balanced net ionic equation describes the copper strip in the Ag⁺ solution?
options: Cu(s) + 2Ag⁺(aq) → Cu²⁺(aq) + 2Ag(s)
Cu(s) + Ag⁺(aq) → Cu²⁺(aq) + Ag(s)
Cu²⁺(aq) + 2Ag(s) → Cu(s) + 2Ag⁺(aq)
Cu(s) + 2Ag⁺(aq) → Cu²⁺(aq) + Ag₂(s)

why.correct: Copper atoms lose 2 electrons each (Cu → Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻) and each Ag⁺ gains 1 (Ag⁺ + e⁻ → Ag). Two Ag⁺ are needed per Cu so electrons lost equal electrons gained; charge is +2 on both sides.
options: Right: 2 electrons lost and 2 gained; atoms and charge balance.
Atoms balance, but charge does not (+1 left, +2 right): electrons lost (2) do not equal electrons gained (1).
This is the reverse; the table shows silver metal does not react with Cu²⁺.
Silver metal is written as Ag(s); it does not form Ag₂ units.

items.q: Based on the table, which metal loses electrons most readily?
options: Mg
Zn
Cu
Ag

why.correct: Magnesium reacts with every other metal ion, so it gives electrons to all of them. Silver reacts with none, so it gives up electrons least readily. Order: Mg > Zn > Cu > Ag.
options: Right: Mg gives electrons to Cu²⁺, Zn²⁺ and Ag⁺.
Zinc reacts with Cu²⁺ and Ag⁺ but not Mg²⁺, so magnesium gives up electrons more readily.
Copper reacts only with Ag⁺.
Silver reacts with none of the solutions, so it loses electrons least readily.

items.q: In the reaction of zinc metal with Cu²⁺(aq), which species is the oxidizing agent?
options: Cu²⁺
Zn
Zn²⁺
Cu

why.correct: Cu²⁺ gains electrons (it is reduced to Cu), and by taking electrons it causes zinc to be oxidized. The species that is reduced is the oxidizing agent.
options: Right: Cu²⁺ is reduced, so it is the oxidizing agent.
Zinc loses electrons; it is oxidized, so it is the reducing agent.
Zn²⁺ is a product, formed when zinc is oxidized.
Copper metal is a product, formed when Cu²⁺ is reduced.

items.q: A zinc strip sits in blue Cu²⁺(aq) until the reaction stops, and the zinc is still present at the end. Predict how each quantity changes.

variables.name: Mass of the zinc strip, not counting the copper coating
variables.why: Zinc atoms are oxidized to Zn²⁺ ions and leave the strip.

variables.name: Intensity of the blue color of the solution
variables.why: Blue Cu²⁺ ions are reduced to copper metal and leave the solution.

variables.name: Number of nitrate ions in solution
variables.why: Nitrate is a spectator ion; it does not react.

variables.name: Number of Zn²⁺ ions in solution
variables.why: Each zinc atom oxidized adds one Zn²⁺ ion.

why.correct: Zn(s) + Cu²⁺(aq) → Zn²⁺(aq) + Cu(s): zinc dissolves, copper ions leave the solution as metal, and nitrate stays put.

items.q: What is the oxidation number of manganese in MnO₄⁻?

mistakes.why: Value: four O at −2 total −8, but the ion has a charge of 1−, not 0. Mn + (−8) = −1, so Mn is +7.
Value: that is the charge of the whole ion. Find Mn from Mn + 4(−2) = −1.

why.correct: Oxygen is −2, so 4 O contribute −8. The sum must equal the ion's charge, −1: Mn + (−8) = −1, so Mn = +7.

items.q: How many electrons does each MnO₄⁻ ion gain in this reaction?
options: 5, because Mn goes from +7 to +2
7, because Mn starts at +7
2, because Mn ends as Mn²⁺
1, because the ion has a 1− charge

why.correct: The oxidation number of Mn falls from +7 to +2, a gain of 5 electrons. That matches the 5 Fe²⁺ each losing 1 electron (Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺).
options: Right: +7 to +2 is a change of 5.
Uses the starting oxidation number alone; the change is what counts.
Uses the final oxidation number alone; the change is 7 − 2.
The charge of the ion is not the number of electrons transferred.

items.q: Using the average of the three trials, what is the molarity of Fe²⁺ in the sample?

mistakes.why: Value: you used a 1 : 1 ratio. Each MnO₄⁻ reacts with 5 Fe²⁺, so multiply the moles of MnO₄⁻ by 5.
Value: you inverted the mole ratio. There are 5 Fe²⁺ per MnO₄⁻, so moles of Fe²⁺ are five times larger, not smaller.

items.q: Why does this titration need no added indicator?
options: The purple titrant shows pink at the first excess
The Fe³⁺ ions formed turn the solution bright purple
Redox reactions give off light when they finish
The acid in the flask changes color at the end point

why.correct: Before the end point every drop of purple MnO₄⁻ is reduced to almost colorless Mn²⁺. Once all the Fe²⁺ is used, the next drop of MnO₄⁻ stays, coloring the solution pale pink.
options: Right: the titrant acts as its own indicator.
Fe³⁺ is pale yellow in this solution, not purple; the color at the end comes from unreacted MnO₄⁻.
These reactions do not glow; the color change is from leftover titrant.
The acid is there to supply H⁺ for the reaction; it does not change color.

items.q: Which statement about this reaction is correct?
options: Fe²⁺ is the reducing agent, as it is oxidized
MnO₄⁻ is the reducing agent, because it becomes Mn²⁺
H⁺ is oxidized, because it ends up in water
Oxygen is reduced, because it ends up in water

why.correct: Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺ raises iron's oxidation number by one: iron loses an electron and is oxidized, so Fe²⁺ is the reducing agent. Manganese is reduced; H and O keep their oxidation numbers (+1 and −2).
options: Right: the species oxidized is the reducing agent.
MnO₄⁻ gains electrons (Mn +7 → +2), so it is reduced and is the oxidizing agent.
Hydrogen is +1 in H⁺ and +1 in H₂O; its oxidation number does not change.
Oxygen is −2 in MnO₄⁻ and −2 in H₂O; it is neither oxidized nor reduced.

items.q: What is the oxidation number of sulfur in H₂SO₄?

why.correct: 2 H at +1 give +2; 4 O at −2 give −8. The compound is neutral: 2 + S − 8 = 0, so S = +6.
options: Right: +2 + S − 8 = 0.
That is sulfur in H₂SO₃ or SO₂, which hold less oxygen; in H₂SO₄ the four O at −2 give −8, so S is +6.
That is sulfur in a sulfide ion or H₂S, where S is bonded to no oxygen.
Ignores the hydrogens: S − 8 = 0 would mean no H atoms.

items.q: Which reactions are redox reactions? Select all that apply.
options: 2H₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2H₂O(l)
NaCl(aq) + AgNO₃(aq) → AgCl(s) + NaNO₃(aq)
Fe₂O₃(s) + 3CO(g) → 2Fe(s) + 3CO₂(g)
HCl(aq) + NaOH(aq) → NaCl(aq) + H₂O(l)

why.correct: In the first, H goes from 0 to +1 and O from 0 to −2. In the third, Fe goes from +3 to 0 and C from +2 to +4. In the precipitation and acid-base reactions no oxidation number changes.
options: Right: both elements change oxidation number.
Every ion keeps its charge; ions only change partners, so no electrons move.
Right: iron is reduced and carbon is oxidized.
An H⁺ moves, not electrons; all oxidation numbers stay the same.

items.q: Combine the half-reactions Al → Al³⁺ + 3e⁻ and Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu into a balanced equation.
options: 2Al + 3Cu²⁺ → 2Al³⁺ + 3Cu
Al + Cu²⁺ → Al³⁺ + Cu
3Al + 2Cu²⁺ → 3Al³⁺ + 2Cu
Al + Cu²⁺ + e⁻ → Al³⁺ + Cu

why.correct: Make electrons lost equal electrons gained: the least common multiple of 3 and 2 is 6. Double the aluminum half-reaction (6e⁻ lost) and triple the copper one (6e⁻ gained), then add; the electrons cancel. Charge: +6 on each side.
options: Right: 6 electrons lost and 6 gained.
Atoms balance but charge does not (+2 left, +3 right); 3 electrons lost but 2 gained.
Swaps the multipliers: 9 electrons lost but 4 gained, and charge +4 left, +9 right.
Electrons never appear in the final equation; they must cancel.

items.q: A student says "in a redox reaction, the oxidizing agent is the substance that gets oxidized." Which reply is correct?
options: No: it takes electrons from another substance, so it is reduced
Yes: its name says that it is the one oxidized
No: the oxidizing agent is the oxygen atom in the reaction
Yes, when oxygen gas is one of the reactants

why.correct: An agent causes the change in something else. The oxidizing agent oxidizes another substance by taking its electrons, so the agent gains electrons and is reduced.
options: Right: the oxidizing agent is reduced.
The name describes what it does to the other reactant, not what happens to it.
Many redox reactions have no oxygen, such as Zn + Cu²⁺; the oxidizing agent there is Cu²⁺.
With or without oxygen gas, the oxidizing agent is the species reduced.

items.q: What is the oxidation number of chromium in the dichromate ion, Cr₂O₇²⁻?

mistakes.why: Value: +12 is the total for both chromium atoms. Divide by 2: each Cr is +6.
Value: 7 O at −2 give −14, and the sum must be −2, not 0. 2Cr − 14 = −2, so Cr = +6.

why.correct: 7 O at −2 give −14. The sum equals the ion's charge: 2Cr + (−14) = −2, so 2Cr = +12 and each Cr = +6.

items.q: A student adds a strip of nickel metal to Cu²⁺(aq) and sees a red-brown coating form. A nickel strip in Zn²⁺(aq) shows no change. Using the ranking Mg > Zn > Cu > Ag for losing electrons, where does nickel fit?
options: Between Zn and Cu
Above Mg
Between Cu and Ag
Below Ag

why.correct: Nickel gives electrons to Cu²⁺, so it loses electrons more readily than copper. It does not give electrons to Zn²⁺, so it loses them less readily than zinc. It fits between Zn and Cu.
options: Right: more readily than Cu, less readily than Zn.
If nickel were above magnesium, it would also reduce Zn²⁺, which it does not.
If nickel were below copper, it could not reduce Cu²⁺, but it does.
A metal below silver would not reduce Cu²⁺; nickel does.
